meta.blurb: A teenage merchant from Venice rides with his father and uncle across deserts, mountains and seas to the court of Kublai Khan. Marco Polo stayed for seventeen years, then came home with stories so wonderful that many people refused to believe them.
meta.bible: Marco Polo: Venetian merchant and traveller, born about 1254, died in January 1324; curious, careful and observant. Niccolò Polo: Marco's father, a merchant. Maffeo Polo: Marco's uncle, a merchant. Kublai Khan: the Great Khan, ruler of the Mongol empire and of China. Mongol: the people of the Khan. Rustichello of Pisa: a writer of romances who wrote down Marco's stories in a Genoese prison. Teobaldo: a church leader at Acre who became Pope in 1271. Kokachin: a seventeen-year-old Mongol princess sent to marry Arghun. Arghun: the Mongol ruler of Persia, who died before she arrived. Ghazan: Arghun's son, whom she married. Donata: Marco's wife. Venice: the trading city on the lagoon where Marco was born. Genoa: Venice's rival; the city of the prison. Curzola: the island where the sea battle of 1298 took place. Constantinople. Acre. Jerusalem. Ayas. Ararat. Caspian. Baghdad. Tabriz. Persia. Saveh. Kerman. Hormuz. Badakhshan. Afghanistan. Pamir. Kashgar. Yarkand. Khotan. Silk Road. Lop. Dunhuang. Ganzhou. Shangdu: the Khan's summer capital, Xanadu. Khanbaliq: the Khan's winter capital, now Beijing. Yunnan. Yangzhou. Yangtze. Grand Canal. Hangzhou: called Quinsai, the City of Heaven. Zaiton: now Quanzhou, a great port. Cipangu: Japan, which Marco never visited. Sumatra. Ceylon: now Sri Lanka. Adam's Peak. India. Trebizond. Black Sea. Mediterranean. Fra Mauro: a Venetian mapmaker of the 1450s. Christopher Columbus. Il Milione: Marco's nickname. Description of the World: the book's own title; it is also called The Travels of Marco Polo. Noah. Buddha. Buddhists. Muslims. Beijing. Quanzhou. Sri Lanka. Marco Polo's sheep: a wild sheep with long horns. Voice and tone: wonder and curiosity, plain and clear; accurate; Marco reports what he saw and what he heard, and the retelling says plainly when something is a story, a doubt or an exaggeration; no gore.

A1A2: Marco Polo was born in Venice, a rich city on the water.
Niccolò and Maffeo rode east and met Kublai Khan, the great Mongol ruler.
The Great Khan welcomed the brothers and asked them many questions about Europe.
Niccolò came home to Venice and met his son Marco for the first time.
In 1271 the three Polos left Venice for the court of the Khan.
They went to Jerusalem and took a little holy oil for the Khan.
They saw a high mountain and a spring that gave black oil.
They passed through Baghdad and Tabriz, two busy cities full of traders.
In Saveh, people showed Marco the tombs of three wise men.
In Kerman they saw fine horses, and then they reached a hot harbour.
The ships at Hormuz looked weak, so the Polos went on by land.
Marco fell ill, but the clean mountain air made him well again.
They crossed the Pamir, a very high land that people call the roof of the world.
They rested in Kashgar and Khotan, green towns in the dry desert.
Next they crossed a desert so wide that it took many days.
They came to China at last and saw many Buddhist temples.
Marco saw the Khan's summer palace, built of white marble.
Kublai Khan welcomed the Polos and was pleased to meet young Marco.
Marco learned the languages of the court and worked for the Khan.
Marco described Khanbaliq, the Khan's big new city with straight streets.
The Khan used paper money, and everyone had to accept it.
In China people burned black stones that made a good, hot fire.
Fast riders carried the Khan's news from one post house to the next.
The Khan planted trees along his roads so that travellers could have shade.
The Khan loved to hunt with big birds and tame leopards.
The Khan sent Marco to Yunnan, far in the south-west of China.
Marco says he ruled the city of Yangzhou for three years.
Marco saw hundreds of boats on the great rivers and canals.
Marco called Hangzhou the finest and most beautiful city in the world.
On the lake in Hangzhou, people ate and laughed together in small boats.
Zaiton was a huge port where ships came from India with spices.
Chinese ships were much bigger and stronger than the ships of Europe.
Marco heard of Japan, an island where a palace had a golden roof.
After many years, the Polos wanted to go home to Venice.
Envoys came from Persia to ask for a princess as a bride.
Fourteen ships left China with the princess, the Polos and many sailors.
On Sumatra Marco saw an animal he called a unicorn.
Marco visited Ceylon, an island with a high mountain and fine rubies.
On India's coast, Marco saw men dive deep into the sea for pearls.
After two years at sea, they reached Hormuz, but many had died.
From Persia, the Polos went home through Trebizond and Constantinople.
Back in Venice, the Polos looked so different that people hardly knew them.
In 1298 Marco fought for Venice at sea, but the Genoese caught him.
In prison Marco met a writer named Rustichello, who wrote down his stories.
Writers copied the book by hand, and it soon spread across Europe.
Marco went home to Venice, married, and had three daughters.
Some people doubt Marco, but many of his stories were true.
Marco Polo died in Venice in 1324, an old man of about seventy.
Later, map makers and Christopher Columbus read Marco's book with great interest.
Today people still read the Travels, and Venice's airport carries his name.
B1B2: Marco Polo was born in Venice around 1254, in a city of canals, boats and busy markets. His father Niccolò and his uncle Maffeo were merchants who had sailed far away, and Marco did not know his father.
Niccolò and Maffeo had sailed to Constantinople and then travelled deep into Asia to trade. Wars blocked the road home, so they went on until they reached the court of Kublai Khan.
The Khan was curious about the Pope, the kings of Europe and the Christian faith. He sent the brothers home with a letter, asking the Pope for a hundred wise men and some holy oil from Jerusalem.
When the brothers reached Venice again, around 1269, Niccolò learned that his wife had died. His son Marco, now about fifteen years old, was waiting there to meet him.
The new Pope was slow to be chosen, so the Polos waited for two years. In 1271 they decided to go, and they took seventeen-year-old Marco with them.
At Acre they spoke with a church leader named Teobaldo, who gave them letters for the Khan. Then they went to Jerusalem, where they filled a small flask with oil from the holy tomb.
Marco writes that people say Noah's ark rests on a huge snowy mountain in Armenia. Near the Caspian Sea he also saw a spring of oil that people used for burning and as medicine.
In Tabriz, in Persia, Marco watched merchants from India, Europe and China buy and sell. He thought it was a very good place to make money.
In the Persian town of Saveh, local people told Marco that the Three Wise Men had lived there. They showed him three tombs, and Marco wrote down the story as he heard it.
The travellers rode south to Kerman, where people mined blue turquoise stones and made fine saddles. After that they came down to the hot port of Hormuz, on the sea.
The boats at Hormuz were sewn together with thread, without nails, and Marco did not trust them. The Polos decided to turn north and take the long road across the land instead.
In Badakhshan, in the north of Afghanistan, Marco became so sick that the group had to stay for about a year. Local people said that mountain air was the best medicine, and he did get well.
The Pamir plateau is so high that Marco says no birds fly there and fires burn less warmly. He also saw huge wild sheep with long curved horns, which scientists later named after him.
These oasis towns lay on the Silk Road, the old trade route between China and the West. In Khotan, Marco saw jade, a smooth green stone that people carved into rings and cups.

Marco says that this desert takes about a month to cross, and that travellers sometimes hear voices calling their names. He thinks evil spirits make them leave the road, so the Polos stayed close together.
After the desert they reached the first towns of China, such as Dunhuang and Ganzhou. Marco saw large Buddhist temples with huge statues, and he stayed in Ganzhou for about a year.
Shangdu, which the English call Xanadu, was the Khan's summer home. Marco describes a marble palace and a park about sixteen miles round, filled with deer and wild animals.
The Khan received them warmly and accepted the holy oil with great respect. When he met the young Marco, he took a liking to him and asked him to enter his service.
Marco was clever and learned several languages and writing systems quickly. The Khan noticed that he did not just do his work but also remembered everything he saw.
The Khan's winter capital was Khanbaliq, which is now Beijing. Marco was amazed by its straight streets, its tall walls and the palace, whose great hall could hold six thousand guests.
Marco was astonished to find that China used paper money, made from the bark of mulberry trees. Each note was stamped with the Khan's red seal, and everyone had to accept it as if it were gold.
In the cold north, Marco saw people burn black stones that gave more heat than wood. These stones were coal, which was little used in Europe at that time, and they also heated the public baths.
The Khan's messengers rode along the main roads, and every twenty-five miles or so they found a post house with fresh horses. Marco says a rider could cover about two hundred miles in a single day.
Marco writes that the Khan ordered trees to be planted along the main roads, to shade travellers and to mark the way. He also kept grain stores, so that people had food when harvests were poor.
Every year the Khan went hunting with thousands of men, trained falcons and tame leopards. Marco says he sometimes travelled in a small wooden room carried on the backs of four elephants.

As the Khan's messenger, Marco travelled to Yunnan, far in the south-west, and reported back on the people there. He saw large crocodiles, which he called serpents, and people who covered their teeth with gold.

In his book, Marco says that the Khan made him governor of the city of Yangzhou for three years. Chinese records do not mention him, so some scholars doubt it, while others think he held a smaller job.
Marco was impressed by the Grand Canal and the Yangtze, where boats carried rice, silk and salt all day long. He claims that there were more ships on one Chinese river than in all of Europe.

Marco calls Hangzhou by the name Quinsai, which he says means City of Heaven. He found canals everywhere and says there were about twelve thousand stone bridges, so tall that ships could pass beneath.
On the beautiful lake of Hangzhou, rich families hired painted boats and enjoyed picnics with music. Marco also saw ten great markets and shops full of fresh fish, fruit, meat and rice wine.
Zaiton, which is now called Quanzhou, was one of the biggest ports in the world. Hundreds of ships arrived from India and Southeast Asia with pepper, pearls and spices.

Chinese ships were bigger than any that Marco knew in Europe, with four masts and many rooms for sailors and merchants. Their hulls were divided into watertight rooms, so one hole would not sink the ship.

Marco never visited Japan, which he calls Cipangu, but he heard that its king had a palace with roofs of gold. He also heard that the Khan sent two huge fleets there, and storms destroyed both of them.
By now the Polos had been in China for about seventeen years and had become rich. They were afraid of what might happen after the old Khan died, but he did not want them to go.
Envoys arrived from the Mongol king of Persia, Arghun, whose wife had just died. The Khan chose a seventeen-year-old princess named Kokachin and agreed that the Polos could take her to Persia by sea.
In about 1291 the fleet of fourteen ships left Zaiton, carrying the princess, the envoys and the Polos. The Khan said goodbye to the Venetians with tears, and they never saw him again.
On the island of Sumatra, the fleet waited about five months for the winds to change. Marco saw a so-called unicorn, but it was a rhinoceros, a heavy and muddy animal and not at all beautiful.
Marco calls Sri Lanka by the name Ceylon, and he praises its rubies as the best in the world. He also describes a high mountain where Buddhists, Muslims and others went on pilgrimage.
On the Indian coast Marco watched divers go down into the sea to collect pearl oysters. He also saw pepper, ginger and cotton, and noted how hot and dry the weather was.

The voyage lasted nearly two years, and Marco writes that most of the people on the ships died on the way. When they reached Persia, they learned that King Arghun was dead, so the princess married his son Ghazan.
The Polos rode on to Tabriz, then to the Black Sea port of Trebizond, and on to Constantinople. From there they took a ship to Venice, which they reached in 1295.

A story, first told long afterwards, says that no one in Venice recognised the three travellers in their rough clothes. It adds that they cut open their coats at a feast and jewels poured out, but this may only be a legend.
Venice and Genoa were rivals, and in 1298 they fought a big sea battle near the island of Curzola. Marco was on a Venetian ship, and when Genoa won, he was taken prisoner and brought to Genoa.
In the Genoese prison Marco met Rustichello of Pisa, a writer of knightly romances. Marco told him about his travels, and Rustichello wrote them down in a French used in Italy, around 1298 and 1299.

The book was called The Description of the World, and scribes copied it by hand in many languages. People nicknamed Marco Il Milione, perhaps because he spoke of millions of things, though no one knows for certain.
Marco was freed in 1299, after Venice and Genoa made peace, and went home to Venice. He married a woman named Donata, had three daughters and lived as a respected merchant.

Critics ask why he does not mention tea, chopsticks or the Great Wall, and Chinese records never name him. On the other hand, much of what he reports, such as paper money, coal and the post system, is accurate.
Marco made his will in January 1324 and died soon afterwards, when he was about seventy. A story says that friends asked him on his deathbed to take back his tales, but he said he had not told half.
Mapmakers used Marco's book, and the famous map of Fra Mauro in the 1450s shows places he described. Christopher Columbus owned a copy and wrote notes in its margins before he sailed west.

The Travels of Marco Polo is still read today, more than seven hundred years after it was written. It reminds us that curious people can cross the world, and that listening carefully is the first step in understanding others.
C1C2: In the thirteenth century, Venice was one of the richest trading cities in Europe, a place of canals and marble churches where ships arrived daily loaded with spices, silk and gossip from distant shores. Into this world Marco Polo was born around 1254, the son of a merchant family whose men were used to travelling for years at a time. His father, Niccolò, and his uncle Maffeo were already far away on a journey, and the boy grew up without once seeing the man whose name he bore.

Years earlier, the two brothers had left Venice to trade in Constantinople, and from there they had pushed eastward through lands that few Europeans had ever seen. When war closed the road behind them, they accepted an invitation to travel on, and so they came at last to the court of Kublai Khan, the ruler of the Mongol empire. No other merchants from Venice had ever stood in that great hall, and the Khan knew it.

Kublai Khan received the brothers kindly and questioned them for hours about the kings, the laws and the religion of the distant West. Curious and shrewd, he decided to send them home as his messengers, carrying a letter that asked the Pope for about a hundred learned men to teach his people. He also wished for a little oil from the lamp that burns at the tomb of Jesus in Jerusalem.

After years on the road, the two brothers finally came back to Venice around 1269, tired, tanned and full of stories nobody could quite believe. Niccolò learned that his wife had died while he was away, and he found himself face to face with a son of about fifteen whom he had never known. The boy, quick and curious, listened to every word his father said about the East.

The Pope had died, and the cardinals took so long to elect a successor that the brothers grew weary of waiting and began to fear that the Khan would suppose they had forgotten him. In 1271 they set out again, and this time they took with them Niccolò's son, Marco, who was about seventeen. Nobody in that little group could have guessed that the boy would not see his home again for twenty-four years.

At the port of Acre the travellers met Teobaldo, a respected church leader, who gave them letters of greeting for the Khan and his blessing for the journey. They then rode to Jerusalem, where they filled a small flask with oil from the lamp at the tomb of Jesus, just as they had promised. The sacred city made a deep impression on the young Marco, who had never been so far from Venice.

Passing through Armenia, Marco heard that Noah's ark had come to rest upon a vast, snow-covered mountain, though no traveller had ever managed to climb high enough to see it. Further east, near the shore of the Caspian Sea, he came across a spring from which oil poured in such quantity that whole shiploads could be filled. The local people burned it in their lamps and rubbed it on their camels as a cure.

Tabriz, in the north of Persia, was a bustling market where merchants from India, Arabia and Europe haggled over silks, pearls and precious stones. Marco, who had been trained in the arts of trade since boyhood, studied the traders closely and noted what each of them valued. In his book he calls it a city so well placed that any merchant who lived there could grow rich.

In the Persian town of Saveh, the villagers told Marco that the three kings who had followed the star to Bethlehem had been born among them, and they showed him their fine tombs. Marco, ever the careful listener, wrote the story down just as it was told to him, without claiming that he could prove it. Such tales, gathered from many mouths, gave his book the flavour of a journey made through legends as well as lands.

At Kerman, in southern Persia, the travellers found miners digging for blue turquoise and craftsmen making saddles and swords for the armies of the East. Beyond the mountains they descended to Hormuz, a scorching harbour on the Gulf where ships arrived from India laden with pearls, spices and cloth. The heat there was so fierce, Marco remarks, that the townspeople retreated into their cellars for part of the day.

The ships that waited at Hormuz had been stitched together with coconut thread instead of nails, and Marco thought them far too flimsy for the open sea. After a short and anxious discussion, the Polos decided to abandon the sea route they had been considering and to go on across Asia by land. It was a choice that would lead them over some of the highest and loneliest places on Earth.

In Badakhshan, among the mountains of what is now northern Afghanistan, Marco fell seriously ill, and the party was obliged to wait there for about a year. The local people assured him that the air of the high valleys would cure him, and, to his relief, they proved right. This long pause, which might have ended the journey, gave the young traveller time to listen and learn.

Next came the Pamir, a plateau so lofty that it has long been called the roof of the world, and Marco says that for twelve days they met neither house nor inn. He notes that fire burns with less heat at such heights, and that the wild sheep there have horns as long as a man's arm. Scientists later honoured him by giving the animal its present name, Marco Polo's sheep.

Descending from the mountains, the travellers reached the oasis towns of Kashgar, Yarkand and Khotan, green islands of orchards and cotton fields set within a sea of sand. These towns lay on the Silk Road, the long chain of trade routes along which silk, jade and ideas passed between China and the West. Marco admired the jade of Khotan, a stone so prized that it was carried across half the world.

To reach China the party had to cross the Lop desert, a waste of sand so wide that Marco says it took the best part of a month to cross. He reports that travellers there sometimes hear voices calling them by name and wander away to their deaths, convinced that the spirits of the desert are leading them. The Polos wisely stayed together, carrying food and water for every day of the crossing.

On the far side of the desert, the travellers finally entered the Chinese lands of the Great Khan, passing through towns such as Dunhuang and Ganzhou. In the temples of Ganzhou, Marco saw enormous statues of the Buddha and heard the chanting of monks, sights that were as new to him as the moon. The Polos remained there for some time, perhaps as long as a year, waiting for the Khan's orders.

At last the travellers came to Shangdu, which poets of a later age would call Xanadu, the cool summer capital of Kublai Khan. Marco describes a palace of white marble and gold, set within a walled park some sixteen miles round, where deer and falcons roamed among streams and green lawns. After three and a half years on the road, the Polos had reached the heart of the Mongol empire.

In about 1275 the three Venetians were led into the Khan's presence, and the old ruler welcomed them like old friends, receiving the holy oil with evident reverence. When Niccolò introduced his son, the Khan studied the young man with interest and soon took him into his own household as a servant and trusted observer. For the next seventeen years Marco would live in the shadow of the most powerful man in Asia.

Marco proved a quick study, mastering several languages and scripts of the Mongol court within a few years. The Khan noticed that his young servant did more than carry out his tasks; he watched, remembered and returned with details that other messengers never bothered to mention. It was exactly the sort of attention that would, one day, fill a famous book.

The Khan spent the winter in Khanbaliq, a newly planned capital on the site of present-day Beijing, whose broad, straight streets crossed one another like the squares of a chessboard. Marco marvels at its tall walls, its twelve gates and the palace in the centre, whose main hall, he says, could seat six thousand guests at a single feast. For a Venetian used to winding alleys and crooked lanes, it was a vision of perfect order.

What astonished Marco most was the Khan's money, which was not made of gold or silver but of paper cut from the inner bark of the mulberry tree. Each piece was stamped with the Khan's red seal, and all his subjects were required to accept it as though it were precious metal. To a merchant from Venice, who had spent his life handling coins, it seemed like a kind of magic.

In the cold northern provinces, Marco saw people digging black stones from the hillsides and burning them in their stoves, where they glowed longer and hotter than any wood. We know this fuel as coal, but to Europeans of the time it was still a curiosity that few had seen. The same fires heated the public baths, where townsfolk washed several times a week.

The Khan's vast empire was held together by a postal service of astonishing speed, with stations at intervals of about twenty-five miles along every main road, each stocked with fresh horses and food. Messengers wore belts hung with bells so that the next station could prepare to receive them, and Marco reports that a rider might cover some two hundred miles in a day. No king or emperor in Europe could have sent word across his lands so fast.

Marco admired the Khan's practical kindness, for he had ordered rows of trees to be planted beside the great roads, giving shade to travellers and marking the way in snowy weather. In years of good harvest the Khan also bought up grain and stored it in great barns, so that in lean years it could be sold cheaply to the hungry. Whatever else he was, Marco concludes, the old ruler cared about the daily welfare of his people.

Each year the old Khan set out upon great hunting expeditions, taking with him thousands of men, hunting falcons and tame leopards trained to chase deer across the open plains. Marco reports that when the Khan was tired, he rode in a wooden room carried upon four elephants, from which he could watch the sport at his ease. At night the whole court camped in tents so splendid that they seemed like a city of silk.

The Khan, who loved news of every corner of his realm, sent Marco on a long mission to Yunnan, a mountainous province far to the south-west. The young envoy saw there great crocodiles, which he described as monstrous serpents with legs, and he was fascinated by a people who covered their teeth with thin sheets of gold. He returned with so many fresh details that the Khan listened, we are told, with greater pleasure than he had felt in years.

Marco's book states that the Khan appointed him governor of the great city of Yangzhou, a post he says he held for three years. No Chinese record mentions a foreigner of his name, which has led some scholars to doubt the claim, while others suppose that he held a lesser office or advised the real governor. Whatever his exact rank, it is clear that he saw the cities of the south at close quarters.

In the south, Marco travelled along the Grand Canal and the mighty Yangtze, which were so crowded with barges that the water seemed to carry a floating market. Boats carried rice, silk, salt and iron to cities that lay hundreds of miles apart. He declares, with obvious exaggeration, that more ships sailed on that one river than on all the seas of Christian Europe.

Of all the cities he visited, none enchanted Marco so much as Hangzhou, which he calls Quinsai and which he translates as the City of Heaven. Canals ran through its streets like silver threads, and he claims that no fewer than twelve thousand stone bridges crossed them, some so high that ships could sail beneath without lowering their masts. It was then probably one of the largest, richest and most refined cities on Earth.

On the shores of the city's lovely lake, Marco watched rich families glide across the water in painted boats, feasting and listening to music while the hills turned blue in the evening. In the ten great markets of the city he found fresh fish, fruit and game piled high, along with rice wine and every spice he knew. He admits that he found the whole place so pleasant that he could scarcely bring himself to leave it.

On the south-eastern coast lay Zaiton, today called Quanzhou, one of the busiest harbours in the world, where merchants from India, Arabia and the islands of the south came to trade. Marco saw ships unloading pepper, pearls and precious wood in such quantities that he was sure no port in Europe could match it. The Khan's officials took a share of every cargo, which helped to pay for the empire.

The sea-going ships of China were larger and stronger than any Marco had seen in the Mediterranean, with four masts, crowds of cabins and room for hundreds of sailors and merchants. Their hulls were divided into watertight compartments, so that a single leak would not sink the vessel, an invention that Europe would not adopt for centuries. Marco, who had grown up among sailors and shipbuilders, studied them with a professional eye.

Marco never sailed to Japan, which he calls Cipangu, but he gathered tales of an island so rich in gold that the king's palace was roofed with the metal and its floors were paved with it. He also recounts the Khan's attempts to conquer the island, when two enormous fleets were wrecked by storms before they could achieve anything. The Japanese called the great winds divine, and historians still remember them by that name.

After some seventeen years at court, the Polos had grown rich and respected, but they also grew homesick, and they feared what might happen to three foreigners once the elderly Khan was dead. Each time they asked leave to depart, however, the Khan refused, for he had come to value his Venetian advisers and was reluctant to part with them. They needed a very good reason to leave, and in the end they found one.

At this moment envoys arrived from Arghun, the Mongol ruler of Persia, whose wife had died and who wished to marry a lady of the Khan's own family. The Khan chose a seventeen-year-old princess named Kokachin, and the envoys, anxious about the dangerous land routes, asked whether the Venetian sailors could help them make the voyage by sea. The Khan, reluctantly, agreed, and gave the Polos golden tablets to guarantee their safe passage.

In about 1291, a fleet of fourteen ships left Zaiton, carrying the princess, the Persian envoys, hundreds of sailors and servants, and the three Venetians with the Khan's gifts. The Khan took his farewell with every sign of emotion, and none of the Polos would ever see him again, for he died only a few years later. Ahead lay an ocean voyage that Marco would remember as the hardest part of his travels.

On the island of Sumatra the fleet was held for about five months, waiting for the seasonal winds to carry it across the Indian Ocean. There Marco saw what he took for the legendary unicorn, but he was disappointed to find that it was an ugly, mud-loving beast with a thick hide, a single horn and a head like a wild boar. Scholars agree that he had seen a rhinoceros, and the legend of the graceful unicorn lost a little of its glamour.

From Sumatra the fleet crossed to Ceylon, the island now called Sri Lanka, which Marco praises for the finest rubies, sapphires and other jewels in the world. He also describes a tall mountain, known as Adam's Peak, to which Buddhists and Muslims alike climbed on pilgrimage, each convinced that the footprint on its summit belonged to their holy man. Marco, with his usual fairness, records both beliefs without choosing between them or mocking either.

Along the southern coast of India, Marco watched divers plunge beneath the sea to gather pearl oysters, holding their breath for as long as they could. He noted the pepper, ginger and fine cotton cloth that filled the markets of every port, and he heard that the divers paid holy men to keep the sharks away with charms. Even in that heat, the coast hummed with trade, and Marco wrote down prices as faithfully as wonders.

The voyage had taken almost two years, and by the time the fleet reached Hormuz, Marco writes, disease and hardship had killed most of the people who had set out. To make matters worse, King Arghun had died while they were at sea, so the princess was married to his son, Ghazan, and the Polos' errand ended in a rather different way than planned. Their duty to the princess done, they could at last turn their thoughts towards the long road to home.

From Persia the Polos rode northward to Tabriz and then to Trebizond, on the shore of the Black Sea, where ships carried them on to Constantinople. A final sea passage brought them in 1295 to Venice, twenty-four years after they had left it, with their precious cargo of stones and stories intact. Marco was now about forty-one, and he had seen more of the world than any other man in his city.

A famous story, first told long after the event, claims that the Polos returned so weather-beaten and strangely dressed that their own relatives refused to let them in. It adds that they invited the family to a feast and then slit open the linings of their coats, from which a stream of jewels poured on the table. There is no evidence for the tale, but it shows how astonished their neighbours were by their wealth.

Venice and Genoa were bitter rivals for the trade of the Mediterranean, and in 1298 their fleets met in a fierce battle off the island of Curzola. Marco, who was on board a Venetian ship, was among the many men captured when the Genoese won the day, and he was carried off to prison in Genoa. It was a bitter blow for a merchant of forty-four, but it turned out to be the most fortunate misfortune of his life.

Among Marco's fellow prisoners was Rustichello of Pisa, a man who had written popular romances about King Arthur and who could always recognise a good story. Marco told him of his journeys and Rustichello wrote them down, in the French that was then the fashionable language of European storytellers. In this dim cell, around 1298 and 1299, the book we know as the Travels was born.

The book, which Marco called the Description of the World, was copied by hand in dozens of versions and translated into many languages, and it reached readers from Italy to England. Many of them thought its marvels exaggerated, and Marco was soon nicknamed Il Milione, perhaps because he was said to talk about millions of things, although the true origin of the name is unknown. Even so, nothing quite like it had ever been written in the whole history of Europe.

When peace was made between Venice and Genoa in 1299, Marco was released, and he went back to his native city, where he settled down to a quieter life. He married a woman named Donata, became the father of three daughters and continued to trade, while his neighbours listened politely to his tales of the Khan. The most famous traveller in the world never left Italy again for the rest of his life.

Critics have long asked why Marco never mentions tea, chopsticks or the Great Wall, and no Chinese record names him, so some scholars suspect that he repeated what other travellers told him. Others point out that his account of paper money, coal, post stations and the ports of the south is accurate and detailed, in ways that are difficult to explain unless he saw them himself. The debate continues to this day, and the honest answer is that nobody can be entirely sure.

Marco made his will in January 1324 and died not long afterwards, at about seventy, in the city where he had been born and where he was buried in a church. A well-known tradition says that his friends begged him on his deathbed to admit that he had invented his marvels, and that he answered that he had not told half of what he had seen. Whether or not the words are really his, they have the ring of the man.

In the following centuries mapmakers drew on his book, and the great map of Fra Mauro, made in the 1450s, shows many places that Marco had described. Christopher Columbus owned a copy of the Travels, in which he scribbled notes in the margins, and he dreamed of reaching the wealth of the East by sailing west. Marco's words had given a whole continent a vivid place in the imagination of Europe.

More than seven hundred years later the Travels is still read, still argued over and still loved, and the airport of Venice carries the name of its author. Whatever the doubters say, the book opened a window on the East for generations of readers who might otherwise never have imagined it. At its best it teaches that curiosity, patience and careful listening can carry a person to the farthest edge of the known world.
